source_text: Sed ut imitationis vocabulum rebus diversis manifestum est communiter convenire; ita generatio vere et proprie generantem substantiam indicat; non proprie autem, sed abusive studiis applicatur. Et tamen quia hic est iam usus loquendi et quod indicarit agnoscitur, et proprietatibus praeiudicium afferre non sinitur. Dicitur ergo diabolus generare peccantes, secundum quod Dominus in Evangelio: Vos, ait, ex patre diabolo estis [n69] . Quo sermone, eum dixit criminosorum patrem, cuius malignitatem convincebantur imitari; et tamen in absoluto est intellegentia, quia per hoc nomen, videlicet patris, nec diabolo sexus, nec hominibus illis aeria sit adscripta substantia. Iam igitur quid confici hinc voluerimus appareat. Si proprie numquam hominem homo iudicaretur imitari, et Apostolus per Adam omnes peccasse dixisset; ego libere praescriberem usu Scripturarum esse Apostolum vindicandum, ut quomodo Dominus diabolum dixerat patrem, qui substantia generare non poterat; ita Apostolus hominem scripsisset imitabilem, ne quid docuisse contra rationem perspicuam crederetur.
pass_a_gloss: But as the vocabulary of imitation is manifestly fitted commonly to diverse things; so generation truly and properly indicates a generating substance; but not properly, but abusively, it is applied to pursuits. And yet because this is already the use of speaking, both what it has indicated is recognized, and it is not allowed to bring a prejudice to properties. The devil is therefore said to generate those sinning, according to what the Lord in the Gospel: You, he says, are from the father the devil. By which speech he said him the father of the criminal, whose malignity they were convicted of imitating; and yet the understanding is in the absolute, because through this name, namely of father, neither a sex has been ascribed to the devil, nor an airy substance to those human beings. Now therefore let it appear what we have wanted to be brought about from this. If properly a human being would never be judged to imitate a human being, and the Apostle had said that all sinned through Adam; I would freely prescribe that the Apostle is to be vindicated by the use of the Scriptures, so that as the Lord had said the devil a father, who could not generate by substance; so the Apostle would have written a human being imitable, lest he be believed to have taught anything against clear reason.

pass_b_english: Just as the word ‘imitation’ plainly applies in common to different things, so ‘generation,’ in its true and proper sense, indicates a substance that begets. It applies to deliberate activities only figuratively, not properly. Yet because this usage is now established, what it indicates is recognized, without allowing it to prejudice the words’ proper meanings. Thus the devil is said to beget sinners, according to the Lord’s words in the Gospel: ‘You are from your father the devil’ (John 8:44). With these words he called the devil the father of criminals who were shown to imitate his malice. Yet the meaning is perfectly clear: the name ‘father’ assigns neither a sex to the devil nor an airy substance to those human beings. Let our intended conclusion now become plain. Suppose a human being were never properly said to imitate another human being, and the apostle had said that everyone sinned through Adam. I would freely insist that scriptural usage must vindicate the apostle. Just as the Lord had called the devil a father, though he could not beget by substance, so the apostle would have described a human being as imitable, to avoid the belief that he taught anything against clear reason.

choices.why: Julian's Rom 5:12 reading: sin passes by copying Adam's example, not by generation/seed.
Julian's target is Augustine's claim that sin is transmitted by begetting; keep generation vs imitation.
